title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.6.5: Improve Prompts Step by Step
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.6.5: Improve Prompts Step by Step

A hands-on lab that improves one prompt in measured steps: structure, output format, reasoning and feedback. Task 1.6, post 5 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-6-5.png — alt: "Skill 1.6.5: Improving prompts step by step"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.6: Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions · Post 5 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 25 minutes.

“Is this return eligible?” looks like a reasonable prompt. Give it a ticket that says “Leaf blower from Sept 20th, never used” and the model has to guess today's date, guess which policy applies, count days in its head, and reply in whatever shape it likes. It gets some right and some wrong, and your code can't tell which. This skill is about improving a prompt in deliberate steps, each one fixing a specific kind of error, and measuring every step.

What AWS says

Skill 1.6.5: Enhance FM performance to refine prompts iteratively and improve response quality beyond basic prompting techniques (for example, by using structured input components, output format specifications, chain-of-thought instruction patterns, feedback loops).

What it means in plain words

  • Structured input components: separate instructions, reference data and user content clearly, for example with labelled XML-style tags.
  • Output format specifications: say exactly what shape the answer must have, such as JSON with named fields, so code can read and check it.
  • Chain-of-thought instructions: ask the model to work through the steps before answering, so multi-step reasoning is less error-prone.
  • Feedback loops: check the answer with code (or a person or another model) and send problems back for the model to fix.

[IMAGE: t1-6-5-iterations.png — alt: "Five versions of one prompt: v0 baseline, v1 structured input, v2 output specification, v3 chain of thought, v4 feedback loop"]

What we're going to do

Run five versions of one prompt over six labelled customer tickets and score each version on two things: the eligibility decision and the day count. Each version adds one technique.

What you'll learn

  • What each technique fixes, and what it doesn't.
  • Why intermediate fields in the output make answers checkable.
  • How to build a feedback loop with deterministic checks.
  • Why you measure on a labelled set instead of judging by a few examples.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 25 minutes, under US$0.05
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; Amazon Nova 2 Lite through the US inference profile
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.6/skill-1.6.5-refinement

The lab

The test set

tickets.json holds six tickets written the way customers write: “3rd Oct”, “Sept 20th”, “1 August”, “25/09”, “two days ago (10 Oct)”. Each is labelled with the right decision and day count, with “today” fixed at 12 October 2026. The traps are deliberate: an unregistered power tool falls back to the 30-day rule, and a clearance mower is never returnable however recent.

Step 1: v0, the first draft

pip install boto3
python refine_lab.py show v0
python refine_lab.py run v0
Is this return eligible?

Bought a hedge trimmer on 3rd Oct, opened it, it's too heavy for me. Can I bring it back?

No policy, no date. The model answers from general knowledge, and the free-text replies have to be parsed by keyword, so even scoring them is approximate.

Step 2: v1, structured input

<policy>General items: 30 days. Garden equipment ...: 14 days. ...</policy>
<today>2026-10-12</today>
<ticket>...</ticket>

Using only the policy, decide whether the return in the ticket is eligible today.

The model now has the facts it needs, clearly separated from the instruction and from the customer's words. Tags also stop text inside the ticket being mistaken for instructions.

Step 3: v2, output format specification

Reply with only this JSON:
{"category": "general|garden|power_registered|power_unregistered|clearance",
 "purchase_date": "YYYY-MM-DD", "days_since_purchase": <integer>,
 "limit_days": <integer or 0>, "eligible": <true|false>, "reason": "<one sentence>"}

Now every answer can be parsed. The intermediate fields matter as much as the decision: when a decision is wrong, you can see whether the category, the date or the arithmetic was at fault.

Step 4: v3, chain of thought

python refine_lab.py show v3
python refine_lab.py run v3
Work it out step by step inside <thinking> tags:
1. Identify the item and its policy category.
2. Find the purchase date and write it as YYYY-MM-DD (assume 2026; numeric dates are DD/MM).
3. Count the days from the purchase date to today.
4. Compare with the category's limit.
Then give only this JSON inside <answer> tags: ...

Asking for the steps, in order, reduces errors in categorising and in date handling. Keeping the reasoning in <thinking> and the result in <answer> means code reads only the answer. The steps also state assumptions explicitly (the year, DD/MM dates) instead of leaving the model to guess.

Step 5: v4, a feedback loop

v4 sends the same prompt as v3, then checks the answer in code:

days = (date.fromisoformat(TODAY) - date.fromisoformat(j["purchase_date"])).days
if days != j.get("days_since_purchase"):
    problems.append(f"From {j['purchase_date']} to {TODAY} is {days} days, not ...")

If anything is wrong, the problems go back to the model as a new user message (“Please fix these problems and answer again”), up to two rounds. Models are unreliable at counting days; code is exact. The loop uses each for what it's good at.

Step 6: Compare

python refine_lab.py compare

The scoreboard shows eligibility and day-count accuracy out of six for each version. Expect a clear upward trend: v0 weakest, v1 and v2 better, v3 and v4 at or near six out of six, with v4 fixing any remaining day-count slips. The exact numbers vary from run to run; the trend is the lesson. Six tickets is a teaching set; a real one would have dozens to hundreds.

The order matters

  1. Give the model the facts, clearly separated (structured input).
  2. Make the output checkable (format specification, or tool use for guaranteed JSON).
  3. Make the reasoning explicit (chain of thought).
  4. Check and correct with code (feedback loop).
  5. Only if all of that falls short, consider a bigger model or fine-tuning.

Change one thing at a time and re-score on the same labelled set, so you know which change helped. That's also what the Skill 1.6.4 test suite is for.

Common pitfalls

  • JSON wrapped in prose or code fences: ask for only the JSON inside tags, strip fences when parsing, or use tool use with a schema.
  • Raising temperature to fix reasoning: it adds variety, not logic. Keep it at 0 for decisions.
  • Endless feedback rounds: cap them (two here) and fall back to a human when the model can't fix the answer.
  • Judging by a few demos: score every version on the same labelled set.

Clean up

Nothing to delete.

What to remember

  • Model mixes up instructions and data → structured input with labelled tags.
  • Code can't parse or check answers → output format specification (or tool use), with intermediate fields.
  • Multi-step reasoning errors → chain-of-thought instructions; reasoning in one tag, answer in another.
  • Answers fail checks code can make → feedback loop: check, send the problems back, cap the rounds.
  • Measure each change on a labelled set; prompt techniques before fine-tuning.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.6 Exam Notes.

References

  • Prompt engineering concepts in Amazon Bedrock

  • Tool use with the Converse API
